title.narrative: Supporting stability in Libya, and mitigating the effects of contagion from the Sahel

description.narrative:
The project¿s overall objective is to support stability in Libya by mitigating the effects of contagion from the Sahel crisis on Libya, advancing the Libyan political process, and supporting international mediators. It will work on these interconnected tracks in a holistic manner, coordinating with the UN, EU and relevant neighbouring or concerned states.

Oc 1 ¿ Both national and local Libyan stakeholders have increased capacity to mitigate the effects of cross-border crises on Libya;

Oc 2 ¿ Libyan conflict actors engage in dialogue processes aimed at long-term stability at the national level and adopt more consensual positions, contributing to violence prevention and reduction;

Oc 3 ¿ The UN and other international mediators have access to a broader array of Libyan stakeholders, including hard-to-reach actors, and the capacity to bring them together in inclusive dialogue processes

comment.narrative: Local actors struggle to communicate with one another and coexist creating tensions and sometimes resulting in locallevel conflict along political tribal or ethnic lines. They are also not wellconnected to international humanitarian efforts that could otherwise benefit their communities. 1.2 Political security and military actors and institutions lack internal coordination to develop a national plan to combat the effects of Sahel instability and sensitive withdrawal of foreign armed groups. Which in turn has amplified the illicit economy and nurtured organized crime posing a security threat to local communities.

Several mediumsized and major facilitated dialogues have taken place over the course of 20192021 particularly under the auspices of the UNled political process. However outcomes of dialogues are not being implemented or adequately manifesting on the ground. level of acceptance of consensual positions expressed by opposing parties engaged in HDled dialogue has been higher in 2020 than it was in 2019 however with the deterioration of the UNled political process acceptance of consensual positions has been low.

title.narrative: Both national and local Libyan stakeholders have increased capacity to mitigate the effects of crossborder crises on Libya

description.narrative: TARGET: 1. By end of June 2025, local actors have the capacity to speak to one another, coexist and work towards reconciliation, and have increased access to international humanitarian efforts both without external intervention. The likelihood of national level conflict fuelled by local conflict will decrease. 1.2: By end of June 2025, national actors have the capacity to cooperate internally on mechanisms to compact the effects of Sahel instability on Libyan borders.Current Value: Ind 1.1: Underlying drivers of conflict and the presence of foreign armed groups in Libya are now being highlighted and one of the priorities of the security track led by the UN. Efforts to address the presence of foreign armed groups are ongoing, but largely uncoordinated. HDs analysis of Sudan/Chad/Niger/Sahel spillover informed bilateral and multilateral engagements (June 2024; Nov 2024; March 2025; and early 2025), including discussions with national security actors and southern stakeholders on sensitivities around foreign armed groups and withdrawal risks. Ind 1.2 The lack of national plan to combat border issues is in the core of the increased in illicit economy, trafficking and illegal migration that impacts the security and safety of immigrants and local communities. HD facilitated exchanges that supported a clearer understanding of border security gaps, foreign armed group sensitivities, and risks of uncoordinated withdrawal; engagements contributed to stabilitysensitive assessments by Libyan and international actors. Ind 1.3: HD engaged with at least 23 organisations/institutions across political, security, economic, local/municipal, and international actors during the reporting period.

comment.narrative: Local actors struggle to communicate with one another and coexist creating tensions and sometimes resulting in locallevel conflict along political tribal or ethnic lines. They are also not wellconnected to international humanitarian efforts that could otherwise benefit their communities. 1.2 Political security and military actors and institutions lack internal coordination to develop a national plan to combat the effects of Sahel instability and sensitive withdrawal of foreign armed groups. Which in turn has amplified the illicit economy and nurtured organized crime posing a security threat to local communities.

Several mediumsized and major facilitated dialogues have taken place over the course of 20192021 particularly under the auspices of the UNled political process. However outcomes of dialogues are not being implemented or adequately manifesting on the ground. level of acceptance of consensual positions expressed by opposing parties engaged in HDled dialogue has been higher in 2020 than it was in 2019 however with the deterioration of the UNled political process acceptance of consensual positions has been low.

Local groups and communities are better represented in national level dialogues, directly or indirectly, by feeding their needs and opinions into a larger scale and higherlevel processes.3.3 The participation of women delegates in intl. peace process is 30% Current value: 3.1 The UN and other international mediators have access to a large array of Libyan political, military and civil society actors. 3.3 Local groups or marginalised constituencies are still largely excluded from the intl. peace process, and when they are present, they often have weak representation and therefore are unable to significantly contribute and are not taken seriously by other more prominent stakeholders. 3.4 The participation of women delegates in intl. peace process is less than 10% (around 5%) (2015 LPD talks, 2017 HoRHCS talks); this has increased with the Libyan Political Dialogue Forum, where participation of women was 23%. Similarly, upon being sworn in in early 2021, the Government of National Unity (GNU) appointed several female ministers, including the foreign minister the first in Libyan history. However, womens participation in the political landscape remains minimal at best.
